cases.description: `aiqe init --print` renders the complete proposed file and writes nothing at all: no aiqe.toml, no machine-local state, no salt.
`aiqe init --yes` writes exactly one repository path, and the scaffold declares no surface and no validator: AIQE does not guess what is quant-critical. A second init refuses rather than overwriting.

A real Unix pseudo-terminal drives the real CLI. The prompt is presented with the validator id, the exact argument vector and the timeout, and states that AIQE does not sandbox the validator or restrict its filesystem or network access. The answer is no: nothing executes, nothing is recorded, and the outcome is CONSENT_DECLINED. An injected prompt callable cannot prove this, because the decision under test is whether AIQE asks at all.

The same real terminal, answered yes. The validator runs exactly once, and consent is recorded against that exact definition digest. A later non-interactive run acts on the recorded consent and runs it again. Then one semantic field of the definition changes: the digest changes with it, the recorded consent no longer applies, and the validator does not run. Consent outlives the task; evidence does not.

A validator that emits eight megabytes on each stream - three orders of magnitude past the retention budget - and then fails. The run completes, the retained output stays within the budget, the evidence record stays small, and the result semantics are unchanged. Output is bounded while it is read, not buffered whole and truncated afterwards.

A validator whose output never stops, under a timeout. Nothing about this run ends on its own: the deadline has to hold, the memory has to hold, and the outcome has to be a failure rather than an unknown. An implementation that read the stream to completion before truncating it would never return.

The boundary of the termination claim, measured rather than worded. A validator spawns a child that calls setsid, leaving the process group AIQE created. The timeout terminates that group; the detached child survives it and finishes on its own afterwards. AIQE terminates the process group it created - it does not contain a process tree, and this case exists so that the stronger, false claim cannot return to the documentation unnoticed.

AIQE's state root already exists, mode 0777. AIQE creates its own state 0700 and does not trust state it did not create: the operation refuses, no validator runs, and the mode is left exactly as it was found. AIQE does not chmod its way out of a trust problem.

The worktree's own state directory is opened to the group after a valid task start. Every later operation refuses: the evidence and the consent record live in there, and a directory the group can write is a directory the group can replace them in.

Genuine recorded consent, in a file mode 0644. This is the component the trust boundary exists for: a consent store somebody else can write is a list of commands they can have executed as this user. It is refused rather than read - and refused even with --allow, because AIQE will not write evidence into a state area it has just decided it cannot trust.

A symlink where the consent store belongs, pointing at a file outside the state area. AIQE refuses, does not follow it to see what is there, and does not replace it - and the target is byte-identical afterwards. Writing through a hostile symlink to 'fix' it would be doing the attacker's work.

The other half of the boundary: ordinary state, created and then reused, keeps working. Run under umask(0) so the modes observed are AIQE's doing rather than the environment's - 0700 directories and 0600 files, on a second run over state that already existed.

A real pseudo-terminal, and an argument vector aimed at it: a screen clear, a cursor home, a carriage return, and a second prompt of the attacker's own. Zero raw control bytes reach the terminal - the argv is rendered escaped, on the line AIQE put it on - the real warning is intact, and the real prompt is still there. Answered no: nothing runs, nothing is recorded.

The same hostile argv, answered yes. The validator runs once, and the consent is recorded against the digest of the argument vector AIQE will actually execute - not the escaped text it printed. If it bound the rendering, two different commands could share one consent, which is the mechanism inverted. Changing a semantic field still ends it.

A validator that fails while printing a screen clear, a carriage return, a bell, a colour change, the word PASS and a prompt of its own. The outcome is FAIL - what a validator says about itself is not evidence - and no raw control byte reaches any human surface. The local evidence keeps the output, escaped and faithful; the default receipt keeps none of it. Rendering is made safe without stripping the record.

negative_controls.description: Check, then edit. The naive tool records that the validators passed and has nothing to compare against afterwards, so its green result survives an edit to the very file it was about. AIQE binds the owned content at check time and recomputes it at receipt time, so the same sequence reports STALE.

Generic tests over a declared quant surface with no required validator bound to its contract. Every validator the repository declares passes, so the naive workflow is green - about a contract nothing in the repository was written to check. AIQE reports COVERAGE_GAP.

Tracked configuration treated as authorization. The naive tool reads aiqe.toml and runs what it declares, so anyone who can land a commit can run a command on the reviewer's machine. AIQE executes nothing without machine-local consent recorded for that exact validator definition.

A validator that edits the file it checks and exits 0. The naive tool records the exit status and calls the result current, so it is green about source that no longer exists. AIQE measures the owned binding on both sides of execution and refuses to produce current evidence.
